prompt: Why can a shared birthday become likely in a surprisingly small group under the independent uniform birthday model?

options.text: Each new person must have a previously unused birthday.
options.explanation: Repeated birthdays are allowed and are the event of interest.

options.text: Half the calendar must be occupied first.
options.explanation: Pair collisions can become likely far before that.

options.text: Every pair of people is a possible match.
options.explanation: The number of pair opportunities grows much faster than the number of people.

options.text: The experiment asks whether someone matches one fixed date.
options.explanation: That is a different, less expansive event.

workedExample: When another person arrives, they can match any earlier person. Counting only people against calendar days misses those many pairs. The complement calculation tracks the diminishing chance of avoiding all earlier dates.

prompt: An analysis reports an expected number of matching birthday pairs greater than one, while the probability of any match is below one. Is that inconsistent?

options.text: No, because probability itself may exceed one.
options.explanation: Probability cannot exceed one; counts can.

options.text: No: some outcomes contain several matching pairs.
options.explanation: A count expectation can exceed one even though every probability is at most one.

options.text: Yes: every expectation must be a probability.
options.explanation: Expectations can describe counts or other numerical quantities.

options.text: Yes: three shared birthdays count as only one pair.
options.explanation: Three people create three unordered pairs.

workedExample: Separate the indicator for any collision from the sum of indicators for all colliding pairs. They agree when there is only one match, but the latter counts multiple matches separately.
